Section 3.1 of Lock⁵ introduces the language that the rest of inference is
built on. A **parameter** is a number that describes a population — a mean
$\mu$, a proportion $p$, a correlation $\rho$, a difference in means
$\mu_1 - \mu_2$ or in proportions $p_1 - p_2$ — and is fixed, though usually
unknown. A **statistic** is the corresponding number computed from a sample
($\bar{x}$, $\hat{p}$, $r$, ...) and **varies from sample to sample**: take a
different random sample and you generally get a different value. The
collection of statistic values over many random samples of the same size is
the **sampling distribution** of the statistic. Two facts make it useful:
statistics from random samples tend to be **centered at the population
parameter** (no systematic **bias** — a biased sampling method produces
statistics centered at the wrong value), and the spread of the sampling
distribution — measured by its **standard error** — shrinks as the **sample
size grows**, so larger samples give more precise estimates.
The exercises below are from *Statistics: Unlocking the Power of Data*
(Lock⁵, 3rd ed., pp. 225–232). Skill Builders 3.1–3.5 identify parameters and
statistics, 3.6–3.11 practice notation, 3.12–3.19 read sampling distributions
off Figure 3.5, and 3.20–3.42 apply the ideas to real settings — several are
simulated below with data already downloaded for earlier sections plus
`ICUAdmissions`, `OttawaSenators2019`, `FloridaLakes`, `NFLContracts2019` and
`RockandRoll2019`. Values that depend on a particular set of random samples
(your samples, our simulated samples) will differ from run to run.

```{python}
#| include: false
import os
from pathlib import Path
_root = Path.cwd()
while not (_root / "_quarto.yml").exists():
    _root = _root.parent
os.chdir(_root)
import numpy as np, pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt, seaborn as sns
sns.set_theme(style="whitegrid")

def sim_props(p, n, reps=10000, seed=2026):
    """Sampling distribution of p-hat from many binomial samples."""
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    return rng.binomial(n, p, reps) / n

def sim_means(data, n, reps=5000, seed=2026):
    """Sampling distribution of x-bar by resampling from a population."""
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    data = np.asarray(data, dtype=float)
    return data[rng.integers(0, len(data), size=(reps, n))].mean(axis=1)
```

::: {.panel-tabset}

## Exercise 3.1

*(Skill Builder 1: parameter or statistic?)* Average household income for all
houses in the US, using data from the US Census.

- **Parameter, notated $\mu$.** The Census covers the entire population of
  interest, so the average describes the population itself.

## Exercise 3.2

Correlation between height and weight for players on the 2020 Brazil World Cup
Team, using data from all players on the roster.

- **Parameter, notated $\rho$.** Data from *all* players on the roster means
  the whole population is measured.

## Exercise 3.3

Proportion of people who use an electric toothbrush, using data from a sample
of 300 adults.

- **Statistic, notated $\hat{p}$.** The value comes from a sample of 300, one
  of many possible samples.

## Exercise 3.4

Proportion of registered voters in a county who voted in the last election,
using data from the county voting records.

- **Parameter, notated $p$.** The voting records give every registered voter
  in the county — the full population.

## Exercise 3.5

Average number of television sets per household in North Carolina, using data
from a sample of 1000 households.

- **Statistic, notated $\bar{x}$.** The average comes from a sample of 1000
  households and would vary from sample to sample.

## Exercise 3.12

*(Skill Builder 3, Figure 3.5.)* Panel (a) shows sample proportions from
samples of size $n = 40$ from a population.

- **Parameter: $p \approx 0.30$** — the dotplot is centered at about 0.30.
- **Standard error $\approx 0.07$** — the sample proportions spread over
  roughly 0.16 to 0.44, about two standard errors on either side of the
  center.

The simulated replica of Figure 3.5 below (using distributions that match each
panel's center and spread) applies to Exercises 3.12–3.19:

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: Simulated replica of Figure 3.5, four sampling distributions
rng = np.random.default_rng(2030)
panels = [("a) proportions, n = 40", sim_props(0.30, 40, reps=5000)),
          ("b) means, n = 30", rng.normal(85, 20, 5000)),
          ("c) means, n = 100", rng.normal(300, 5, 5000)),
          ("d) proportions, n = 180", sim_props(0.80, 180, reps=5000, seed=2031))]
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(7, 4))
for ax, (lbl, v) in zip(axes.flat, panels):
    ax.hist(v, bins=28, color="#4c72b0")
    ax.set_title(lbl, fontsize=9)
    ax.set_yticks([])
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

- **(a)** The parameter is $p$, the **proportion of all US smartphone users
  who have downloaded an app**.
- **(b)** The best estimate is the sample proportion

## Exercise 3.23

**Florida Lakes.** Florida has over 7700 lakes. We wish to estimate the
correlation between the pH levels of all Florida lakes and the mercury levels
of fish in the lakes; for a sample of $n = 53$ lakes the correlation is
$-0.575$.

- **(a)** Parameter: $\rho$, the **correlation between pH and mercury for all
  Florida lakes**. Statistic: $r = \mathbf{-0.575}$, the correlation in the
  sample of 53 lakes, which is the best estimate.
- **(b)** An estimate is necessary because measuring every lake is
  impractical — to compute $\rho$ exactly we would have to test **all 7700+
  lakes** for both pH and fish mercury levels.

*Data:* `data/ch03/FloridaLakes.csv`, from
<https://www.lock5stat.com/datasets3e/FloridaLakes.csv> — the sample
correlation reproduces $-0.575$:

```{python}
#| echo: false
fl = pd.read_csv("data/ch03/FloridaLakes.csv")
pd.Series({"n": len(fl), "r (pH, AvgMercury)": round(fl["pH"].corr(fl["AvgMercury"]), 3)}).to_string()
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: Mercury level of fish versus pH for a sample of 53 Florida lakes
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5, 3))
ax.scatter(fl["pH"], fl["AvgMercury"], color="#4c72b0", s=22)
r = fl["pH"].corr(fl["AvgMercury"])
ax.text(6.3, 1.25, f"r = {r:.3f}", fontsize=9, color="#c44e52")
ax.set_xlabel("pH of lake")
ax.set_ylabel("Average mercury (mg/kg)")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

## Exercise 3.24

**Topical Painkiller Ointment.** Insurance records show the average copayment
for a month's supply of topical painkiller ointment for regular users is \$30;
a sample of $n = 75$ regular users found a sample mean of \$27.90.

- **(a)** The population average $\mu = 30$ dollars is a **parameter**; the
  sample average $\bar{x} = 27.90$ dollars is a **statistic**.
- **(b)** The dotplot of 1000 sample means of size $n = 75$ would be roughly
  symmetric and bell-shaped (averages of 75 copayments vary less and more
  smoothly than individual copayments), and it would be **centered at 30
  dollars**, the population mean.
- **(c)** There would be **1000 dots**, and **each dot is one sample mean** —
  the average copayment from a single random sample of 75 regular users.

## Exercise 3.25

**Don't Text and Drive!** At least 14% of distracted-driving traffic fatal-
ities are clearly linked to cell phone use. For samples of $n = 500$ such
fatalities, Figure 3.6 shows the sampling distribution of the proportion
caused by cell phone use (centered at $p = 0.14$, standard error about
0.015).

Give the notation and value of each sample statistic, and whether it is
**likely** or **very unlikely** to occur just by random variation:

- **(a)** 38 of 500 deaths: $\hat{p} = \frac{38}{500} = 0.076$ — **unlikely**
  (about 4 standard errors below 0.14, below every plotted value).
- **(b)** 64 of 500: $\hat{p} = 0.128$ — **likely** (less than one standard
  error below 0.14).
- **(c)** 76 of 500: $\hat{p} = 0.152$ — **likely** (less than one standard
  error above 0.14).
- **(d)** 105 of 500: $\hat{p} = 0.210$ — **unlikely** (well above the largest
  plotted values).

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: Simulated sampling distribution of p-hat for n = 500 with p = 0.14, marking the four outcomes
ph = sim_props(0.14, 500, reps=10000)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 3))
ax.hist(ph, bins=40, color="#4c72b0")
for x, lbl in [(0.076, "a"), (0.128, "b"), (0.152, "c"), (0.210, "d")]:
    ax.axvline(x, color="#c44e52", ls="--", lw=1)
    ax.text(x, ax.get_ylim()[1] * 0.92, lbl, ha="center", fontsize=9, color="#c44e52")
ax.set_xlim(0.05, 0.23)
ax.set_xlabel("Sample proportion")
ax.set_ylabel("Frequency")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

## Exercise 3.26

**What Proportion of Canadian Adults Graduate High School?** The 2016 Canadian
Census shows that 81.7% of Canadian adults have a secondary or equivalent
degree.

- **(a)** $p = \mathbf{0.817}$ (a parameter — the census covers the whole
  population).
- **(b), (c)** For a sample of $n = 500$ the sample proportion $\hat{p}$ will
  vary from sample to sample; one sample might give $\hat{p} = 0.82$, four
  more might give values like 0.80, 0.83, 0.81 and 0.84.
- **(d)** The simulated sampling distribution below (10,000 samples of
  $n = 500$) is centered at $p = 0.817$ with **standard error
  $\approx 0.017$**.

```{python}
#| echo: false
ph = sim_props(0.817, 500, reps=10000)
pd.Series({"Center": round(ph.mean(), 3), "Standard error": round(ph.std(ddof=1), 4)}).to_string()
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: Simulated sampling distribution of p-hat for n = 500 with p = 0.817
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3))
ax.hist(ph, bins=30, color="#4c72b0")
ax.axvline(0.817, color="#c44e52", ls="--", lw=1)
ax.text(0.8185, ax.get_ylim()[1] * 0.9, "p = 0.817", fontsize=9, color="#c44e52")
ax.set_xlabel("Sample proportion")
ax.set_ylabel("Frequency")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

## Exercise 3.27

**Average Household Size.** The US Census lists the average household size as
2.61. Figure 3.7 shows four dotplots of 1000 sample means, two from random
samples and two from a biased sampling method.

- **(a) Biased: B and C.** These two dotplots are **not centered at 2.61** —
  the average household size in their samples systematically misses the
  population value, which is the signature of bias (random samples are
  centered at the parameter). For example, dotplot B (centered low) could
  come from sampling only residents of a retirement community, where most
  people live alone; a sample that misses large households is biased
  downward.
- **(b)** Of the two unbiased dotplots (A and D), **A goes with $n = 100$**
  (more spread out) and **D goes with $n = 500$** (tighter around 2.61) —
  larger samples produce less variable sample means.

## Exercise 3.28

**Proportion of US Residents Less Than 25 Years Old.** The US Census
indicates $p = 0.35$; Figure 3.8 shows sampling distributions of the sample
proportion for $n = 20$, $n = 100$ and $n = 500$.

- **(a) A ↔ $n = 20$** (spread over about 0.1–0.7), **B ↔ $n = 100$**
  (about 0.25–0.45), **C ↔ $n = 500$** (about 0.3–0.42) — the larger the
  sample, the tighter the dotplot.
- **(b)** Off by more than 0.10: with $n = 20$ this is only about one standard
  error — **not very surprising** (it happens often); with $n = 100$ it is
  about 2 standard errors — **somewhat unusual but possible**; with $n = 500$
  it is almost 5 standard errors — **very surprising, extremely unlikely**.
- **(c)** Off by 0.05 or more: with $n = 20$ (about half a standard error) and
  $n = 100$ (about one standard error) this is **common**; with $n = 500$
  (about 2.4 standard errors) it is **unusual, though it might occur
  occasionally**.
- **(d)** Increasing the sample size shrinks the standard error, so larger
  samples give **more precise** estimates of $p$.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: Simulated sampling distributions of p-hat with p = 0.35 for n = 20, n = 100 and n = 500
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(7, 2.8), sharey=True)
for ax, n, sd in zip(axes, [20, 100, 500], [2026, 2027, 2028]):
    q = sim_props(0.35, n, reps=10000, seed=sd)
    ax.hist(q, bins=24, color="#4c72b0")
    ax.set_title(f"n = {n}", fontsize=9)
    ax.set_yticks([])
    ax.set_xlim(0, 0.75)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

## Exercise 3.29

**Mix It Up for Better Learning.** Fourth-graders studied either mixed problem
sets (average grade 77) or one equation at a time (average grade 38).

- **Parameter:** $\mu_m - \mu_o$, the **difference in the mean grade between
  all fourth-graders who study mixed problems ($\mu_m$) and those who study
  one equation at a time ($\mu_o$)**.
- **Statistic:** $\bar{x}_m - \bar{x}_o$, the difference in sample means.
- **Best estimate: $77 - 38 = \mathbf{39}$ points** in favor of mixed
  practice.

## Exercise 3.30

**What Proportion of Adults and Teens Text Message?** A study of $n = 2252$
adults found 72% of cell phone users text; a study of $n = 800$ teens found
87% of teen cell phone users text.

- **Parameter:** $p_A - p_T$, the **difference in the proportion of cell phone
  users who text, between all adults ($p_A$) and all teens ($p_T$)**.
- **Statistic:** $\hat{p}_A - \hat{p}_T = 0.72 - 0.87$, the difference in
  sample proportions.
- **Best estimate: $\mathbf{-0.15}$** — a smaller proportion of adults than
  teens text (or equivalently, teens exceed adults by 15 percentage points).

## Exercise 3.31

**Hollywood Movies.** Figure 3.9 shows one boxplot of budget data (millions of
dollars) for a single random sample of $n = 30$ movies and one boxplot of a
sampling distribution of 1000 sample means of budgets, also from samples of
size 30.

- **(a) Boxplot B is the single sample; Boxplot A is the sampling
  distribution.** Individual movie budgets vary enormously (0 to 250+ million,
  heavily right-skewed), while averages of 30 movies vary much less and sit in
  a narrow band — only Boxplot A shows that small spread.
- **(b)** In the single-sample boxplot each value is **the budget of one
  Hollywood movie in the sample**; $n = 30$ values are included, ranging from
  about 1 to 150 million dollars, with $\bar{x} \approx 60$ million dollars
  (heavily influenced by a few big-budget films).
- **(c)** In the sampling-distribution boxplot each value is **a sample mean
  from one sample of 30 movies**; $n = 1000$ means are included, ranging from
  about 20 to 95 million dollars, centered at $\mu \approx 52$ million
  dollars — our best estimate of the average budget for all Hollywood movies
  of this period.

*Data:* `data/ch01/HollywoodMovies.csv`, from
<https://www.lock5stat.com/datasets3e/HollywoodMovies.csv> — one sample of 30
versus 1000 sample means:

```{python}
#| echo: false
bud = pd.read_csv("data/ch01/HollywoodMovies.csv")["Budget"].dropna()
rng = np.random.default_rng(2026)
one = rng.choice(bud.to_numpy(), 30, replace=False)
means = sim_means(bud, 30, reps=1000, seed=2027)
pd.Series({"One sample: min, max, mean": f"{one.min():.1f}, {one.max():.1f}, {one.mean():.1f}",
           "1000 means: min, max, mean": f"{means.min():.1f}, {means.max():.1f}, {means.mean():.1f}",
           "Population mean": round(bud.mean(), 2)}).to_string()
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: One random sample of 30 movie budgets versus the sampling distribution of 1000 sample means
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 2.8))
ax.boxplot([means, one], vert=False, widths=0.5)
ax.set_yticklabels(["Sampling distribution (1000 means)", "One sample (30 budgets)"])
ax.set_xlabel("Budget (millions of dollars)")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

## Exercise 3.32

**What Percent of the US Population Are Senior Citizens?** People 65 and older
constituted $p = 0.13$ of the US population in 2010. Figure 3.10 shows
sampling distributions of the sample proportion for samples of size 100 and
size 1000.

- **(a)** Both distributions are **centered at 0.13** — the population
  proportion.
- **(b)** For $n = 100$: minimum $\approx 0.05$ and maximum $\approx 0.21$.
  For $n = 1000$: minimum $\approx 0.09$ and maximum $\approx 0.17$.
- **(c)** Roughly half the full spread: **SE $\approx 0.035$** for $n = 100$
  and **SE $\approx 0.011$** for $n = 1000$ (the simulations below give 0.034
  and 0.011).
- **(d)** A sample proportion of 0.17 is about 1.2 standard errors above
  0.13 — **not very surprising from a sample of size 100**, but almost 4
  standard errors above the center — **quite surprising from a sample of size
  1000**.

```{python}
#| echo: false
q100 = sim_props(0.13, 100, reps=10000)
q1000 = sim_props(0.13, 1000, reps=10000, seed=2027)
pd.Series({"SE (n = 100)": round(q100.std(ddof=1), 4),
           "SE (n = 1000)": round(q1000.std(ddof=1), 4)}).to_string()
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: Simulated sampling distributions of p-hat with p = 0.13 for n = 100 and n = 1000
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(7, 2.8), sharey=True)
for ax, q, lbl in zip(axes, [q100, q1000], ["n = 100", "n = 1000"]):
    ax.hist(q, bins=24, color="#4c72b0")
    ax.axvline(0.13, color="#c44e52", ls="--", lw=1)
    ax.set_title(lbl, fontsize=9)
    ax.set_yticks([])
    ax.set_xlim(0.04, 0.22)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

  means of **3282.6** and **1132.5** students — values will vary from sample
  to sample, and both happen to fall below the population mean because
  enrollment is strongly right-skewed (one huge college can dominate a small
  sample).
- **(c)** The mean enrollment for the entire population of 1141 two-year
  colleges is $\mu = \mathbf{4050}$ students. The sample means of parts (a)
  and (b) are quite far from it — with only $n = 10$ from such a skewed
  population, a single sample mean can be off by a lot.
- **(d)** The distribution of many sample means of size $n = 10$ would be
  **centered at 4050**.

start of the 2019 season.

  of **\$4.69 million** and **\$0.88 million** — values will vary from sample
  to sample.
- **(c)** The mean for the entire population of players is
  $\mu = \mathbf{\$3.03}$ million. With samples of only 5 from a heavily
  right-skewed population (one star quarterback can dominate a sample), the
  sample means are quite inaccurate — the first overshot the population mean
  and the second undershot it.

```{python}

i2 = rng.choice(len(nf), 5, replace=False)

                 nf.loc[i2, ["Player", "YearlySalary"]].assign(Sample="2")])
```

## Exercise 3.35

**A Sampling Distribution for Two-Year College Enrollments.** Generate a
sampling distribution of sample means with $n = 10$ from the `Enrollment`
values of `CollegeScores2yr`, then repeat with $n = 60$.

- **(a)** With $n = 10$ the distribution is **somewhat right-skewed** (it
  inherits the skew of the enrollment population), **centered at
  approximately 4050**, with **standard error around 1900** (our simulation:
  1940).
- **(b)** With $n = 60$ the distribution is **more symmetric (more
  bell-shaped)**, still **centered around 4050**, with **standard error
  around 760** (our simulation: 783) — four times the sample size cuts the
  standard error roughly in half.

```{python}
#| echo: false
m60 = sim_means(enr, 60, seed=2027)

```

```{python}

    ax.hist(q, bins=36, color="#4c72b0")
    ax.axvline(enr.mean(), color="#c44e52", ls="--", lw=1)
    ax.set_title(lbl, fontsize=9)

    ax.set_xlim(0, 12000)
```

  (\$488,000) and the largest is **\$35 million**.
- **(b)** In our simulated distribution for $n = 5$, the sample means range
  from about **\$0.56 million to \$14.12 million** (values will vary) — huge
  spread compared with the population range, because a single star player can
  dominate a sample of 5.
- **(c)** The standard error for $n = 5$ is about **\$1.96 million**.
- **(d)** With $n = 50$ the standard error drops to about **\$0.63 million**,
  and the means range only from about \$1.31 to \$5.71 million — ten times
  the sample size shrinks the standard error by roughly
  $\sqrt{10} \approx 3.2$.

```{python}

           "Means n = 5: min, max, SE": f"{m5.min():.2f}, {m5.max():.2f}, {m5.std(ddof=1):.2f}",
           "Means n = 50: min, max, SE": f"{m50.min():.2f}, {m50.max():.2f}, {m50.std(ddof=1):.2f}"}).to_string()
```

  about 0.063**.

## Exercise 3.41

**A Sampling Distribution for Females in the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame.**
Using all 329 inductees as the population ($p = 0.158$), take many samples and
record the proportion female or with female members.

- **(a)** For $n = 10$: **SE ≈ 0.115**; in our simulation the farthest sample
  proportion was $\hat{p} = 0.70$ (a sample with 7 of 10 female-related
  inductees), about **0.54 away** from 0.158. Values will vary.
- **(b)** For $n = 20$: **SE ≈ 0.080**; the farthest $\hat{p}$ was 0.50, about
  **0.34 away**.
- **(c)** For $n = 50$: **SE ≈ 0.052**; the farthest $\hat{p}$ was 0.38, about
  **0.22 away**.
- **(d)** Increasing the sample size shrinks the standard error and pulls the
  extreme sample proportions closer to $p$ — **larger samples give more
  accurate estimates** of the population proportion.

```{python}
#| echo: false
rows = []
for n, sd in [(10, 2026), (20, 2027), (50, 2028)]:
    q = sim_means(fem, n, reps=10000, seed=sd)
    far = q[np.abs(q - fem.mean()).argmax()]
    rows.append({"n": n, "Standard error": round(q.std(ddof=1), 3),
                 "Farthest sample proportion": round(far, 2),
                 "Distance from p": round(abs(far - fem.mean()), 2)})
pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("n").to_string()
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: Sampling distributions of the proportion female or with female members for n = 10, 20 and 50
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(7, 2.6), sharey=True)
for ax, n, sd in zip(axes, [10, 20, 50], [2026, 2027, 2028]):
    q = sim_means(fem, n, reps=10000, seed=sd)
    ax.hist(q, bins=20, color="#4c72b0")
    ax.axvline(fem.mean(), color="#c44e52", ls="--", lw=1)
    ax.set_title(f"n = {n}", fontsize=9)
    ax.set_yticks([])
    ax.set_xlim(-0.02, 0.8)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```
